title: What Is a Contradiction? A Framing Piece
subtitle: How to distinguish a real contradiction from a difficult passage or textual variant.
summary: A contradiction occurs when two claims cannot both be true in the same sense, time, and respect. Differences in detail are not automatically contradictions, but a proposed harmony must genuinely fit the texts. Quran 4:82 openly invites this test; careful comparison should apply the same standard to Quranic and biblical passages.

sections.title: The Question in Brief
sections.body: A contradiction means two claims cannot both be true in the same sense, time, and respect. A difference is not automatically a contradiction. A harmony must still fit the texts. Quran 4:82 invites this test. The same standard should apply to Quran and Bible.

sections.title: A Textbook Case: Who Incited David's Census?
sections.body:
In 2 Samuel 24, David orders a census treated as sinful. A plague follows. The chapter opens: "Again Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”" (2 Samuel 24:1, World English Bible). In the later account, 1 Chronicles 21 opens: "Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel." (1 Chronicles 21:1, World English Bible).

The Hebrew verb comes from *sut*, "to incite" or "entice." The WEB and KJV use "moved." NIV, ESV, and NASB use "incited." The verb is the same. The subject differs.

Samuel-Kings and Chronicles are separate works. Samuel-Kings reached near its present form during or after the sixth-century BC exile, using older sources. Chronicles is later, often dated to the fourth century BC, and retells history with different choices and theology. The census change is substantial: who incited David?

Gleason Archer treats it in *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties*. Sara Japhet discusses it critically. The case is genuine and long recognized across theological schools.

sections.title: The Quran's Challenge: Quran 4:82
sections.body:
The Quran asks whether people have reflected on it. If it were from other than God, they would find much contradiction within it (4:82). Coherence is part of its case. Muslims should welcome questions and avoid special pleading.

Coherence does not mean identical detail. Context, general and specific statements, and stages of law can explain tension. Explanations must fit Arabic and the text.

sections.title: A Biblical Example: David's Census
sections.body:
Second Samuel 24:1 attributes the census impulse to the Lord. 1 Chronicles 21:1 attributes it to Satan. Christian interpreters may say God permitted an act Satan prompted. Critical scholars may see later theological revision.

Both readings can be stated. The question is whether the levels of agency arise naturally from the passages or were added only to reconcile them.

sections.title: Use the Same Standard
sections.body: A difference, apparent tension, and formal contradiction are different. Apply the distinction to Quran and Bible. State the strongest harmony and its assumptions. An imagined scenario is not a solution.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions About "Contradiction"
sections.body:
Lists of Bible or Quran contradictions often skip classification. They may count textual variants, harmonizable difficulties, interpretations, and logical contradictions together. That inflates rhetoric, not evidence.

Calling a problem harmonizable is not always an excuse. Some harmonies are weak. The census reading can draw on dual agency elsewhere: Job 1-2, 1 Kings 22, and Genesis 50:20. That is stronger than an ad hoc rescue, though it still needs judgment.

Quran 4:82 does not stop Muslim study of tension. Ibn Qutayba's hadith work and *mushkil al-Qur'an* literature show a long tradition of serious analysis.

Calling something interpretation is not evasion. Scholars debate every stable ancient text. Debate alone does not prove a defect.

sections.title: Why Coherence Matters
sections.body: Human authors can err or revise. Revelation from the all-knowing God should withstand reflection. Quran 4:82 is a meaningful test when Muslims apply it honestly and reject weak answers.

sections.title: Why This Matters: What Is a Contradiction? A Framing Piece
sections.body: Fair comparison needs stable definitions. Islam welcomes examination because the Quran calls people to reflect on its coherence. A strong case identifies real tensions and does not inflate harmless differences. This honesty supports the Quran's invitation to recognize revelation.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Is every difference a contradiction?
A: No. A contradiction asserts and denies the same claim in the same sense and time. Different angles or emphasis can both be true.

Q: What is a textual variant?
A: It is a wording difference among manuscripts or readings. A contradiction concerns truth: two claims cannot both be true.

Q: Is harmonization always an excuse?
A: No. Some harmonies are weak. A pattern found elsewhere, such as dual agency in Job, 1 Kings 22, and Genesis 50, is stronger than an isolated rescue.

Q: What does Quran 4:82 claim?
A: It claims internal coherence, not that no verse will surprise a first reader or that it answers questions outside the Quran.

Q: Why compare 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1?
A: The Lord is named in one and Satan in the other. Christian dual-agency harmony and critical revision are both testable readings.

Q: How should difficulties be examined?
A: State them strongly. Then assess the best Christian and Islamic responses by stable definitions.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties** — Gleason L. Archer. Evangelical harmonization reference.
- **I & II Chronicles: A Commentary** — Sara Japhet. Critical study of Chronicles.
- **Jesus, Interrupted** — Bart D. Ehrman. Historical-critical study of biblical differences.
- **Ta'wil Mukhtalif al-Hadith** — Ibn Qutayba. Classical study of difficult hadith reports.

bibleVerses.text: Again Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he moved David against them, saying, “Go, count Israel and Judah.”
Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel.

Micaiah said, “Therefore hear Yahweh’s word. I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.
Yahweh said, ‘Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?’ One said one thing; and another said another.
A spirit came out and stood before Yahweh, and said, ‘I will entice him.’
Yahweh said to him, ‘How?’
He said, ‘I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’
He said, ‘You will entice him, and will also prevail. Go out and do so.’
Now therefore, behold, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you.”
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is today, to save many people alive.

faq.question: Is every difference between two accounts of the same event a contradiction?
faq.answer: No. A contradiction requires the same claim to be asserted and denied, in the same sense, at the same time. Two accounts that describe the same real event from different angles, with different emphasis or compression, can both be true — that is a harmonizable difficulty, not a contradiction.

faq.question: What is the difference between a textual variant and a contradiction?
faq.answer: A textual variant is a disagreement between manuscripts, or reading traditions, over the wording of the same passage — a question about transmission history, like the debated ending of Mark's Gospel or differences among the Quran's authenticated qira'at. A contradiction is a claim about truth: that two assertions cannot both be true in any sense. They are different kinds of question entirely.

faq.question: Doesn't calling something "harmonizable" just mean scholars are making excuses?
faq.answer: Sometimes a harmonization is weak. But a harmonization that draws on a pattern independently attested elsewhere in the same text, such as the Bible's recurring pattern of God permitting a lesser agent to act toward a sovereign purpose, seen in Job, 1 Kings 22, and Genesis 50, is a stronger, more principled argument than an isolated after-the-fact rescue, and should be weighed on its own merits.

faq.question: What does Quran 4:82 actually claim?
faq.answer: That the Quran's own text, examined carefully, does not contain the kind of internal drift a single human author would be expected to produce writing across changing circumstances over twenty-three years. Muslim scholarship reads it as a claim about the Quran's internal coherence, not as a claim that no verse will ever look surprising on first reading, and not as a verdict on questions outside the Quran's own text.

faq.question: Why are 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 compared so often?
faq.answer: Because the case is unusually compact: one act, inciting David to order the census, is attributed to the LORD in 2 Samuel 24:1 and to Satan in 1 Chronicles 21:1. Christian interpreters propose a dual-causation harmony in which God permits a secondary agent, while historical-critical readers see Chronicles revising the earlier theology. The pair is useful because both readings can be stated clearly and tested against the texts.

faq.question: How Should Specific Difficulties Be Examined?
faq.answer: Specific, well-known difficulties between Islam and Christianity should be stated as strongly and honestly as their sharpest critics state them, then assessed through the strongest responses from Christian and Islamic scholarship using these definitions.

furtherReading.title: Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties
furtherReading.author: Gleason L. Archer
furtherReading.note: A standard evangelical harmonization reference that illustrates the dual-causation approach to difficult biblical passages.

furtherReading.title: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (Old Testament Library)
furtherReading.author: Sara Japhet
furtherReading.note: A leading critical commentary examining how the Chronicler reworked material inherited from Samuel-Kings, including the census narrative's shift in the identity of the inciting agent.

furtherReading.title: Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible
furtherReading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
furtherReading.note: A widely read presentation of the historical-critical approach to differences among biblical books.

furtherReading.title: Ta'wil Mukhtalif al-Hadith
furtherReading.author: Ibn Qutayba
furtherReading.note: A classical ninth-century work devoted to systematically resolving apparently conflicting hadith reports, illustrating the depth of the Islamic tradition's own internal tools for handling textual difficulty.
